title: Unleveled fully homomorphic encryption from LWE alone
formal: Does ordinary polynomial-modulus decisional LWE, with the parameter convention below, imply a classical compact fully homomorphic encryption scheme whose keys are generated without an evaluation-depth bound, secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries without any additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumption?
definitions: Fix the following ordinary LWE assumption: for every fixed integer \(c\ge 3\) and polynomial sample count \(M(d)\), let \(q(d)\) be the least prime at least \(d^{c}\), let s be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{d}\), let A be uniform in \(Z_{q}^{M(d)\times d}\), and let the coordinates of e be independent integers with probability proportional to \(\exp (- \pi z^{2}/(4d))\), reduced modulo q. The ensembles (A,As+e mod q) and \((A,u)\), for independent uniform \(u\in Z_{q}^{M(d)}\), are computationally indistinguishable against nonuniform classical circuits of size polynomial in d. Thus the error distribution is the discrete Gaussian \(D_{Z,2\sqrt{d}}\); only ordinary independently generated LWE samples are assumed hard. The FHE scheme has uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms \(Gen(1^{\lambda})\to\)(pk,evk,sk), \(Enc(pk,b)\), Eval(evk,\(C,c_{1},\ldots ,c_{t}\)), and \(Dec(sk,c)\), with bit plaintexts and Boolean circuits over AND, OR and NOT. Gen takes no circuit-size or depth bound. There is one fixed polynomial P such that keys, fresh bit ciphertexts, evaluated one-bit ciphertexts and the time to decrypt a valid output are bounded by \(\mathrm{P}(\lambda )\), independently of C and t. Evaluation is polynomial-time in \(\lambda\) and its total input length. For every polynomial p, uniformly over all circuits C of size and input count at most \(p(\lambda )\) and all input bits \(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t}\), decrypting Eval on independent encryptions of these bits equals \(C(b_{1},\ldots ,b_{t})\), except with negligible probability over generation, encryption and evaluation. Ordinary decryption is correct with negligible error. Given both pk and evk, every nonuniform polynomial-size classical adversary has negligible advantage in distinguishing an encryption of 0 from one of 1. Negligible means smaller than \(\lambda ^{-a}\) eventually for every \(a>0\). No subsequent secret-key assistance, ideal oracle, external trusted setup, superpolynomial adversary-hardness assumption, functional-encryption assumption or obfuscation assumption is allowed. This fixes a polynomial-modulus version of “standard LWE”; it does not assume any encryptions of secrets or correlated hints are secure.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: Determine whether ordinary LWE alone supports compact encrypted computation at arbitrary polynomial depth with one fixed key set.

importance.reason: A central foundational gap in fully homomorphic encryption, separating established leveled LWE constructions from reusable fixed-depth-independent keys and their extra security assumptions.

progress.text: Brakerski–Vaikuntanathan establish leveled FHE from ordinary LWE; the journal abstract explicitly separates the additional weak circular-security assumption for removing levels.
Brakerski’s quantum-FHE paper records a classical bootstrappable GSW-style scheme with polynomial modulus, citing Brakerski–Vaikuntanathan; this does not eliminate the separate key-cycle issue.
Micciancio’s slides pose the ordinary-LWE circular-security question and distinguish FHE from full composability.
Bitansky–Solomon bootstrap via functional encryption under polynomial hardness assumptions; extra primitives remain, and nonuniform security needs an additional complexity assumption.
Wang–Huang–Tang remove CRS and circularity assumptions in a dynamic multi-key construction whose formal setup still takes L.
Liu and coauthors’ quantum proposal retains \(\mathrm{L}+1\) key layers and a quantum evaluator, outside the target model.

status_note: No classical unleveled compact FHE construction from the specified ordinary LWE assumption alone was found through 11 September 2026. Functional-encryption constructions use additional assumptions. The inspected February and April 2026 no-circularity proposals retain explicit level bounds; the latter also uses quantum evaluation. This card fixes polynomial-modulus LWE, nonuniform classical security and fresh-input FHE correctness.

context_blocks.text: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on encrypted data and return an encrypted answer. Compactness makes this substantive: the client should decrypt a short answer, rather than receive the original ciphertexts together with the whole circuit and perform the computation itself. Here all four algorithms are classical, and the ciphertext for one output bit remains bounded by a fixed polynomial in the security parameter.

The order of choices is the heart of the problem. In a leveled scheme, the user first chooses a maximum depth L and generates keys suitable for that level. This can support every circuit up to L without revealing the data. The present question asks for one key-generation algorithm that receives only the security parameter and supports every polynomial-depth circuit later supplied to the evaluator. Choosing \(\mathrm{L}=\lambda ^{10}\) during setup still leaves deeper polynomial computations outside the guarantee.

Lattice ciphertexts generally include small errors that hide the plaintext. Homomorphic operations transform the desired message and these errors together. Once the error exceeds the decryption tolerance, the output may no longer decode correctly. Gentry’s bootstrapping idea refreshes a ciphertext by homomorphically evaluating a decryption circuit, with the secret key itself provided in encrypted form. Micciancio’s teaching slides explain both this noise issue and the associated circular-security question.

A chain of independent keys avoids the immediate circularity. Encrypt the secret key at level i under the public key at level \(i+1\), then use the next level to refresh the current ciphertext. The usual hybrid proof can replace those encryptions in reverse order because the chain has an endpoint. But the public material grows with the number of refreshes planned in advance. Closing the chain into a cycle reuses a bounded collection of keys and changes the security argument.

Brakerski and Vaikuntanathan’s construction makes the distinction explicit in its journal abstract: ordinary LWE gives leveled FHE, while removing the depth restriction uses an additional weak circular-security assumption. Later bootstrapping work supports polynomial-modulus parameters and polynomial lattice approximation factors. Improvements in error growth and efficiency do not themselves justify exposing the secret-key encryptions needed to reuse the keys.

The requested proof need not avoid bootstrapping, or even avoid encrypted keys. It must justify the actual public evaluation information using ordinary LWE alone. Conversely, it is not enough to prove that some artificially designed CPA-secure encryption scheme becomes insecure when encrypting its own key. Such a counterexample refutes an automatic upgrade for every scheme; it does not rule out designing a particular FHE scheme with a valid ordinary-LWE proof.

Bitansky and Solomon obtain FHE without circular-security assumptions using functional encryption, under polynomial hardness assumptions. This is a significant positive result for a broader assumption set. In their ITCS 2023 construction, the available functional-encryption instantiation uses assumptions including LPN, bilinear SXDH and shallow pseudorandom generators, in addition to the LWE-based homomorphic component. The basic theorem protects against uniform adversaries; their nonuniform extension requires an additional worst-case complexity assumption. Neither version establishes LWE alone under the convention here.

Recent claims also require checking the formal setup. Wang, Huang and Tang’s February 2026 dynamic multi-key scheme advertises avoiding a common reference string and circular security. Definition 2.2 nevertheless gives Setup the depth parameter L, and the construction chooses its dimension and modulus using L. Its stated compactness also permits dependence on L. This is a leveled guarantee, even though the number of participating keys can change dynamically.

Liu and coauthors’ April 2026 quantum homomorphic proposal also advertises classical LWE and no circular-security assumption. Its Section 3.4 uses \(\mathrm{L}+1\) independent key layers; a later discussion explicitly preallocates L evaluation gadgets. It therefore retains a level bound, and its evaluator performs quantum operations. These scope differences already prevent it from settling the classical, depth-independent target; this review does not validate its separate efficiency or quantum-security claims.

There is a further definitional distinction between evaluating one arbitrary circuit on fresh ciphertexts and repeatedly evaluating new circuits on the resulting ciphertexts. Micciancio’s slides show that correctness for the first task does not automatically imply correctness for the second. This card asks for the usual fresh-input FHE guarantee. Establishing full composability would be an additional accomplishment, rather than an implicit condition that makes the target harder.

A solution would remove a central gap between the clean assumption used to prove the security of leveled lattice encryption and the extra assumption used to reuse a fixed key set indefinitely over polynomial computations. It would clarify the foundation of FHE independently of practical parameter optimization, and could improve the assumptions of constructions that use unrestricted encrypted computation as a component.

sentences: Fully homomorphic encryption lets a server evaluate computations on encrypted data and return a compact encrypted answer.
Leveled schemes choose their keys after fixing a maximum computation depth.
This project asks whether ordinary polynomial-modulus LWE can support keys generated without such a depth bound while preserving compactness.
It specifically excludes additional circular-security or key-dependent-message assumptions often associated with bootstrapping.
A solution would establish whether unrestricted encrypted computation follows from the stated LWE assumption with no extra security hypothesis.
